491: Chapter 4  Underwater Image Object Detection Based on an Improved YOLOv8
493: Underwater object detection is one of the core tasks of underwater visual perception systems, and has important application value in fields such as marine biological monitoring, autonomous navigation of underwater robots and marine resource exploration. However, the underwater imaging environment is complex: as light propagates through water it is jointly affected by multiple factors such as scattering, absorption and refraction, causing underwater images generally to suffer from degradation phenomena such as low contrast, colour shift and blurred edges. These visual defects severely constrain the ability of object detection algorithms to extract effective features.
494: From the perspective of this thesis's overall "enhancement-detection" framework, the FSCIN super-resolution reconstruction network proposed in Chapter 3 has already systematically improved image quality with respect to the above degradation problems: through frequency-spatial collaborative modelling it reconstructs originally low-quality underwater images into high-quality images with clearer texture, more accurate colour and more complete edge information, achieving an optimal PSNR of 30.04dB at x2 magnification on the USR-248 dataset and a reconstruction accuracy of 24.03dB at x8 magnification with only 2.45GFLOPs, verifying the effectiveness and efficiency of the front-end enhancement module. The work of this chapter takes the sharpened images output by Chapter 3 as direct input, and builds an accurate underwater object detection model on the basis of these higher-quality images, realising the second stage of the complete processing chain "original image -> super-resolution sharpening -> clear image -> object detection -> detection result". Through this cascaded design, the object detection model can extract more effective target features from images with richer detail and higher contrast, thereby significantly improving the detection recall rate and localisation accuracy for tiny underwater targets. At present, one-stage detection methods represented by YOLOv8 still face the following main limitations when applied directly to underwater scenes [39][43]: first, YOLOv8 performs feature extraction with convolutional neural networks at its core, and being limited by the local receptive field it struggles to model long-range dependency relationships in the image, with somewhat deficient capability for capturing global contextual information; second, the original C2f module has insufficient fine-grained feature representation capability for small targets, and detection accuracy for tiny targets (such as sea urchins and scallops) under low-visibility underwater conditions is limited; third, although PAN-FPN-type structures can enhance multi-scale information fusion [38], in complex underwater scenes the appearance differences, occlusion and background interference of targets at different scales still weaken the model's adaptive fusion capability, making it difficult to simultaneously accommodate the detection requirements of targets at different scales.
495: Addressing the above problems, this chapter proposes an improved YOLOv8 underwater image object detection model, designing a Fine-Grained Feature Extraction Module (FFEM) to replace the C2f module in the original YOLOv8. This module is composed collaboratively of three functional sub-modules: the Channel-Spatial Adaptive Enhancement Module (CAEM) precisely focuses on target edges and texture details through convolution and channel-spatial attention mechanisms; the Mamba-based global perception module (Visual SSM, VSSM) uses a visual state space model to model long-range dependencies and capture global contextual information; and the Multi-Scale Cross-Attention Fusion Module (MCFM) adaptively fuses the two feature streams through a dynamic weighting mechanism, outputting a
497: highly discriminative fine-grained feature representation. Experiments on the URPC2021 underwater object detection dataset show that, compared with
498: the original YOLOv8, the improved model raises mAP50 by 1.8 percentage points (0.855 -> 0.873) and raises small-target APs by 1.1 percentage points (0.166 -> 0.177), verifying the effectiveness of this chapter's method in the second stage of the "enhancement-detection" cascaded framework. The content of this chapter is arranged as follows: Section 4.2 introduces the related basic techniques; Section 4.3 details the overall architecture of the improved network and each functional module; Section 4.4 presents the experimental setup and result analysis; Section 4.5 analyses the influence of super-resolution reconstructed images on object detection performance; Section 4.6 is the chapter summary.
501: The YOLO (You Only Look Once) family of algorithms is the representative approach in the current field of one-stage object detection. By modelling the detection task as a direct regression problem, it predicts target categories and bounding-box coordinates simultaneously within a single forward inference pass, achieving a good balance between detection speed and accuracy. YOLOv8 is a more recent version in this series, with a number of systematic improvements in network structure and training strategy.
502: In terms of the backbone network, YOLOv8 adopts a newly designed C2f module to replace the C3 module of the previous generation. The C2f module splits the input feature map into two branches - one passed through directly, the other undergoing deep feature extraction through multiple Bottleneck blocks - and finally concatenates and fuses all intermediate outputs, improving gradient flow while maintaining computational efficiency. In terms of feature fusion, YOLOv8 inherits the PAN-FPN structure, achieving bidirectional fusion of multi-scale features through a top-down semantic path and a bottom-up detail path, enhancing detection capability for targets at different scales. In terms of the detection head, YOLOv8 adopts a decoupled head design, processing the classification branch and the regression branch separately, reducing mutual interference between the two tasks and improving detection accuracy.
503: Although YOLOv8 performs excellently in general object detection tasks, its backbone network is dominated by local convolution operations and lacks the capability to explicitly model global dependency relationships; the C2f module has limited fine-grained feature representation capability when handling small underwater targets. It is therefore necessary to make targeted improvements to YOLOv8 for the image characteristics of underwater scenes, in order to improve its detection robustness in complex underwater environments.

522: This chapter makes targeted improvements on the basis of the original YOLOv8 architecture, replacing the C2f module in the backbone network and neck network with the designed Fine-Grained Feature Extraction Module (FFEM), while the remaining structure is kept unchanged, as shown in Figure 4.2.

The outputs of the two branches undergo preliminary fusion through element-wise addition, giving the intermediate feature X', which is then dynamically weighted and fused by MCFM, finally outputting the fine-grained feature FFEM. 556: Because the receptive field of a traditional CNN is confined to a local neighbourhood, it is difficult to establish dependency relationships between distant pixels of an image within a single layer, and it lacks effective modelling capability for the global blur phenomenon in underwater images caused by scattering. The Mamba-based global perception module (VSSM) introduces a visual state space model, encoding long-range temporal and spatial dependencies with implicit state variables, overcoming the constraint of the convolutional local receptive field and being better suited to capturing the global contextual features of underwater images. As shown in Figure 4.6, VSSM contains two parallel processing branches, and performs gated fusion of the two outputs through a Hadamard product.
557: Main branch (global context extraction): the input feature X first passes through a linear transformation (Linear) to adjust the distribution dimensions of the feature space; then it passes through a depthwise separable convolution (DWConv), which extracts local spatial information while maintaining lightweight computational characteristics; afterwards a SiLU activation function (i.e. the Swish function, f(x) = x . sigma(x)) introduces non-linear representational capability; next a two-dimensional state space model (2D-SSM) performs a serialised scan of the features, modelling global spatial dependencies in the horizontal and vertical directions with linear complexity; finally layer normalisation (LN) stabilises the feature distribution, yielding the global-perception intermediate feature
558: Gating branch (adaptive information screening): a linear transformation and SiLU activation are applied in turn to the input feature X, generating the gating weight X2:
560: Gated fusion output: the two outputs are fused through a Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication); the gating mechanism adaptively
561: screens and retains the effective components of the global contextual information, and finally a linear transformation completes the adjustment of feature dimensions, giving the module output:
563: This design dynamically screens the global features extracted by the 2D-SSM through a gating mechanism, effectively filtering out interference from underwater background noise and improving feature robustness while maintaining global perception capability.

567: This chapter carries out experimental verification on the URPC2021 underwater object detection dataset. This dataset was released by the 2021 China Underwater Robot Professional Competition and contains a total of 7,600 annotated underwater images, covering four typical classes of underwater target: sea cucumber, sea urchin, scallop and starfish. The various target classes differ considerably in size, morphology, texture and background complexity, and can reasonably comprehensively reflect the detection challenges of real underwater scenes.
568: The dataset annotations use the YOLO format; each label file contains the target category index and normalised bounding-box coordinates. Before the experiments, the samples were uniformly inspected, filtering out images with severe blur, excessive occlusion or abnormal annotation, to ensure the usability of the training and test data. Finally, the training set (6,080 images) and test set (1,520 images) were split in a ratio of 8:2, and all model comparisons were completed under the same split.

581: This chapter uses standard evaluation metrics from the object detection field to evaluate model performance, including IoU, Precision, Recall, AP, mAP50, mAP50-95, and AP metrics for targets of different scales. The above metrics comprehensively reflect model performance in terms of localisation accuracy, false-detection control, missed-detection control and multi-scale detection capability.

593: To verify the effectiveness of this chapter's improved method, comparative experiments were conducted with the original YOLOv8 as the baseline model, completing training and testing under the same dataset split and the same training hyperparameter settings, ensuring the fairness and reliability of the comparison results. The only difference between the two methods is that this chapter's method replaces the C2f module in the original YOLOv8 with the proposed fine-grained feature extraction module, while the remaining network components are kept identical.
594: In terms of training strategy, the standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimiser is used in combination with a cosine annealing learning-rate schedule. Multiple data augmentation techniques are used during training, including random horizontal flipping, colour jitter (adjusting brightness, contrast and saturation) and Mosaic augmentation, in order to improve the model's generalisation capability under the variable conditions of underwater scenes.    4.4.4 Quantitative Analysis

597: 4.2 it can be seen that the improved model raises mAP50 from 0.855 to 0.873, and mAP50-95 from 0.516 to 0.530, indicating that the model maintains higher detection accuracy across different IoU thresholds. Small-target detection
599: capability is clearly enhanced, with APs rising from 0.166 to 0.177; this is mainly attributable to the channel-spatial
600: attention mechanism of CAEM within the FFEM module, which effectively focuses on target edges and details and improves localisation accuracy for small targets such as sea urchins and scallops. Large-target detection performance also improves, with APl rising from 0.664 to 0.675, showing that VSSM's effective modelling of global contextual information provides support for the complete perception of large targets. However, medium-target detection declines slightly, with APm falling from 0.402 to 0.391; this may be because the multi-scale convolution module has a certain scale bias in extracting medium-target features, which requires further optimisation. Overall, the improved model outperforms the original YOLOv8 in comprehensive detection accuracy and in small-target and large-target detection capability, providing a clear direction for subsequent model optimisation. Overall, this chapter's improved method achieves clear improvements in both comprehensive detection metrics and small-target accuracy, verifying the effectiveness of FFEM in the underwater object detection task.

604: To investigate the difference in convergence between the YOLOv8 network models before and after improvement, this thesis conducted training and validation experiments on the original YOLOv8 and the improved YOLOv8 respectively under the same dataset split and hyperparameter settings; their training loss, validation loss and main evaluation metric curves are shown in Figure 4.8 and Figure 4.9. As the figures show, the bounding-box loss (BBox Loss), classification loss (Classification Loss) and distribution focal loss (DFL) of both models drop rapidly in the early stages of training and then gradually stabilise, indicating that the models can effectively complete feature learning and enter a converged state. Compared with the original YOLOv8, the improved model's training loss curve declines more smoothly overall; although the validation loss fluctuates slightly in the later stages, it remains stable overall, indicating that the improved structure does not introduce obvious training instability. From the trend of the evaluation metrics, Precision, Recall, mAP50 and mAP50-95 all rise rapidly in the early stages of training and gradually level off in the middle and later stages, indicating that detection performance gradually stabilises as training proceeds. The improved YOLOv8 is slightly better than the original model on final Precision, mAP50 and mAP50-95, indicating a certain improvement in target localisation and category discrimination. Overall, under the same dataset and hyperparameter conditions the improved YOLOv8 maintains good convergence stability and achieves a certain improvement in final detection accuracy, providing experimental evidence for its application in underwater object detection tasks.
